lead: A short column under axial load carries its load through concrete and longitudinal steel acting together. Design chooses steel area so the factored load stays below the section capacity, then adds ties to hold the bars straight and prevent buckling. The idea exists because columns are the one member whose failure can bring down a whole frame. You meet it in every RCC building: a G+3 apartment, a school hall, a factory shed. The arithmetic is short, but the concrete area must exclude the steel.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 for limit state and partial safety factors, and 5.1 to confirm the column is short.

blocks.text: An axially loaded column carries load along its centroidal axis. In a short column, buckling does not govern; the section fails when concrete and steel reach their design strengths. The limit state of collapse in compression gives a simple addition of concrete capacity and steel capacity. The code permits this axial formula when the minimum eccentricity is at most 0.05 times the lateral dimension. If eccentricity is larger, the column bends and 5.3 applies.

blocks.where: Pu is factored axial load in N; fck is concrete cube strength in N/mm²; fy is steel yield strength in N/mm²; Ac = Ag − Asc is concrete area in mm²; Ag is gross area in mm²; Asc is steel area in mm².

blocks.text: The stress 0.4 fck is the design compressive strength of concrete in a column. It is lower than the 0.446 fck used for beam flexure. The steel stress is 0.67 fy. Steel must be between 0.8% and 6% of Ag. The minimum steel resists accidental bending and shrinkage; the maximum avoids congestion and keeps concrete carrying most of the load.

sections.h3: Design steps for a tied short column

blocks.text: Start with the factored load and the chosen section. Confirm from 5.1 that the column is short and that the minimum eccentricity e_min is within the axial limit. For the worked example, e_min = 20 mm on the 300 mm side, greater than 0.05 × 300 = 15 mm. Strictly, the section must then be designed for the minimum eccentricity moment; the axial formula is used here as the usual exam simplification, and the small moment is covered by the design margin. In practice such columns are checked with 5.3.

items: Write Pu in N. Note fck, fy and Ag = b × D in mm².
Find the steel needed from Asc = (Pu − 0.4 fck Ag) ÷ (0.67 fy − 0.4 fck). This comes from substituting Ac = Ag − Asc in the axial formula.
Apply the limits: Asc must be at least 0.008 Ag and at most 0.06 Ag. Raise a small value to the minimum; if the required value exceeds 6%, enlarge the section.
Choose bars: pick a diameter and a whole number of bars so the provided area is just above the required area. Check the percentage again.
Check capacity with the provided area: Ac = Ag − Asc, then Pu,cap = 0.4 fck Ac + 0.67 fy Asc. It must be at least Pu.

Design ties: diameter ≥ max(6 mm, largest longitudinal bar diameter ÷ 4). Spacing ≤ min(least lateral dimension, 16 × smallest longitudinal bar diameter, 40 × tie diameter, 300 mm). Use a convenient diameter and spacing within these limits.

blocks.text: Keep cover as required for durability. Cover is not part of the strength formula, but it fixes the bar positions. For a tied column, the ties are the only lateral restraint, so their spacing and diameter are not optional.

The axial formula is a strength check, not a slenderness check. A stocky column can still fail by buckling if it is slender; that is why 5.1 comes first. The formula also assumes the load is axial with only the minimum eccentricity. Real frames push moments into columns from beam loads, wind and earthquakes. Those moments need the interaction diagram of 5.3, even when the axial load is high. In ordinary gravity frames, many inner columns are close to axial, so this chapter covers a large share of columns in a building. Corner and edge columns usually carry moment and need the next chapter. Always recheck capacity with the bars actually provided, because rounding to a standard diameter changes the area. A small change in bar diameter can move capacity by tens of kilonewtons.

spec.title: Axial column design
spec.aria: Design flow from factored load 1200 kN, to chosen section 300 by 400 mm with gross area 120,000 square mm, to required steel area where minimum governs, to four 20 mm bars, to 8 mm ties at 300 mm spacing.

examples.question: Design the longitudinal steel and ties for a short tied rectangular column 300 mm × 400 mm carrying a factored axial load of 1200 kN. Use M20 concrete and Fe415 steel. Take cover 40 mm.
steps: Pu = 1200 kN = 1,200,000 N. fck = 20 N/mm², fy = 415 N/mm². Ag = 300 × 400 = 120,000 mm². Minimum Asc = 0.008 × 120,000 = 960 mm². Maximum Asc = 0.06 × 120,000 = 7200 mm². For the 300 mm side, e_min = 20 mm is greater than 0.05 × 300 = 15 mm. Strictly, the section must then be designed for the minimum eccentricity moment; the axial formula is used here as the usual exam simplification, and the small moment is covered by the design margin. In practice such columns are checked with 5.3.
Asc needed = (1,200,000 − 960,000) ÷ 270.05 = 888.72 mm². This is below 960 mm², so the minimum governs. Required Asc = 960 mm².
Try 4 bars of 20 mm: Asc = 4 × π × 20² ÷ 4 = 1256.64 mm². Percentage = 1256.64 ÷ 120,000 × 100 = 1.047%, between 0.8% and 6%.
Ties: diameter ≥ max(6 mm, 20 ÷ 4 = 5 mm) = 6 mm; use 8 mm. Spacing ≤ min(300 mm, 16 × 20 = 320 mm, 40 × 8 = 320 mm, 300 mm) = 300 mm. Use 8 mm ties at 300 mm c/c. Cover 40 mm.
examples.answer: Use 4 bars of 20 mm (Asc = 1256.64 mm², 1.047% of Ag) with 8 mm ties at 300 mm c/c; the section capacity is 1299.35 kN, greater than the factored load of 1200 kN.
examples.check:
import math
Pu = 1200e3
fck = 20.0
fy = 415.0
b = 300.0
D = 400.0
Ag = b * D
min_Asc = 0.008 * Ag
max_Asc = 0.06 * Ag
Asc_req = (Pu - 0.4 * fck * Ag) / (0.67 * fy - 0.4 * fck)
Asc_gov = max(Asc_req, min_Asc)
n = 4
dia = 20.0
Asc_prov = n * math.pi * dia**2 / 4.0
Ac = Ag - Asc_prov
Pcap = 0.4 * fck * Ac + 0.67 * fy * Asc_prov
tie_spacing = min(b, 16.0 * dia, 40.0 * 8.0, 300.0)
print(f'{Asc_req:.2f}')
print(f'{min_Asc:.2f}')
print(f'{Asc_prov:.2f}')
print(f'{Pcap/1000.0:.2f}')
print(f'{tie_spacing:.2f}')

traps: Using Ag instead of Ac = Ag − Asc in the concrete term. This overcounts concrete and gives a lower, unsafe steel area.
Stopping at the calculated Asc when it is below 0.8% of Ag. The minimum steel must be enforced.
Borrowing 0.446 fck from beam flexure for a column. The axial column formula uses 0.4 fck.
Taking tie diameter as one-quarter of the smallest bar. The rule is one-quarter of the largest longitudinal bar, and never less than 6 mm.

Using 16 times the largest bar, or forgetting the 40 × tie diameter and 300 mm caps, for tie spacing. The spacing limits are the least lateral dimension, 16 times the smallest longitudinal bar, 40 times the tie diameter, and 300 mm; the smallest governs.

quiz.q: Write the axial capacity formula for a tied short column with minimum eccentricity.
quiz.a: Pu = 0.4 fck Ac + 0.67 fy Asc, with Ac = Ag − Asc.

quiz.q: State the minimum and maximum longitudinal steel percentages of gross area for a column.
quiz.a: Minimum 0.8% of Ag; maximum 6% of Ag.

quiz.q: Why is Ac = Ag − Asc rather than Ag in the axial formula?
quiz.a: Steel and concrete cannot occupy the same space. The gross area is concrete plus steel, so concrete area is gross area minus steel area. Using Ag would count the steel area twice.

quiz.q: A 250 mm × 250 mm column carries Pu = 600 kN. Use M20 and Fe415. Find the required Asc and state whether minimum steel governs.
Design ties for a column with 6 bars of 25 mm diameter and least lateral dimension 350 mm.
quiz.a: Tie diameter ≥ max(6 mm, 25 ÷ 4 = 6.25 mm); use 8 mm. Spacing ≤ min(least lateral dimension 350 mm, 16 × smallest bar = 16 × 25 = 400 mm, 40 × tie diameter = 40 × 8 = 320 mm, 300 mm) = 300 mm. Use 8 mm ties at 300 mm c/c.

quiz.q: A designer uses Ag in the concrete term and finds a smaller Asc. Is the result safe? Explain in one line.
quiz.a: No. Using Ag counts concrete under the steel, overestimates concrete capacity, and gives less steel than the correct formula. The column is under-designed.

quiz.q: A 300 × 400 column has 4 bars of 20 mm. If the factored load rises from 1200 kN to 1350 kN, is the existing section safe? Use M20 and Fe415.
quiz.a: Existing capacity from the worked example is 1299.35 kN. 1350 kN is greater, so the section is not safe by the axial formula. Enlarge the section, increase the concrete grade, or add steel.

quiz.q: Why does the code put a maximum limit of 6% on longitudinal steel?
quiz.a: To avoid congestion, keep concrete placing and compaction possible, and ensure concrete carries a reliable share of load. Very high steel also makes the column brittle and makes beam-column joints difficult.

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice, column design software builds interaction diagrams for both axes and checks every load combination, not just axial load. Modern codes push toward performance-based design and high-strength materials. Fibre-reinforced concrete and steel jackets are used to strengthen old columns. Search for column interaction diagram, confinement reinforcement, IS 456 column design, or axial capacity of RC column to go further.
